title: Your Brain at Night, Explained
desc: Every night you switch off for hours, but your brain doesn't. In this complete guide we follow your brain through one whole night: why it fights sleep at bedtime, why you stay up when you're exhausted, why waking at 3 AM is more normal than you think, why worries feel huge in the dark, plus the falling jolt, dreams, sleep paralysis, memory, the brain's night-time cleaning crew, night owls, phones, and what actually helps you sleep better.
sources: Borbély, A. A. (1982). A two process model of sleep regulation. Human Neurobiology, 1, 195-204. Retrospective: Borbély et al. (2016/2022), The two-process model of sleep regulation: beginnings and outlook, Journal of Sleep Research (PMC9540767).

Porkka-Heiskanen, T., Strecker, R. E., Thakkar, M., Bjorkum, A. A., Greene, R. W. & McCarley, R. W. (1997). Adenosine: a mediator of the sleep-inducing effects of prolonged wakefulness. Science, 276, 1265-1268.
Drake, C. et al. (2013). Caffeine effects on sleep taken 0, 3, or 6 hours before going to bed. Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine (AASM press release, 14 Nov 2013).

Lavie, P. (1986): first description of the 'forbidden zone' for sleep in the hours before habitual bedtime, as described in: The forbidden zone for sleep is more robust in adolescents compared to adults, Frontiers in Sleep (2023).
Kroese, F. M., De Ridder, D. T. D., Evers, C. & Adriaanse, M. A. (2014). Bedtime procrastination: introducing a new area of procrastination. Frontiers in Psychology, 5, 611.

Kühnel, J., Syrek, C. J. & Dreher, A. (2018). Why don't you go to bed on time? A daily diary study on the relationships between chronotype, self-control resources and the phenomenon of bedtime procrastination. Frontiers in Psychology.
Scientific American: It goes by the name 'bedtime procrastination,' and you can probably guess what it is (on 'revenge bedtime procrastination').
The Conversation: An unbroken night's sleep is a myth. Here's what good sleep looks like (sleep cycles of roughly 90 minutes, brief awakenings).
Ekirch, A. R. (2001), historical paper on segmented sleep ('first sleep' and 'second sleep'), and his book At Day's Close (2005).
Wehr, T. A. (1992). In short photoperiods, human sleep is biphasic. Journal of Sleep Research.

Tubbs, A. S., Fernandez, F.-X., Grandner, M. A., Perlis, M. L. & Klerman, E. B. (2022). The mind after midnight: nocturnal wakefulness, behavioral dysregulation, and psychopathology. Frontiers in Network Physiology, 1.
Yoo, S.-S., Gujar, N., Hu, P., Jolesz, F. A. & Walker, M. P. (2007). The human emotional brain without sleep: a prefrontal amygdala disconnect. Current Biology, 17(20), R877-R878.
van der Helm, E. et al. (2011). REM sleep depotentiates amygdala activity to previous emotional experiences. Current Biology.
plan: Why your brain fights sleep: sleep pressure (adenosine), the body clock, the 'forbidden zone' before bedtime, caffeine.
Revenge bedtime procrastination: why you stay up when you're exhausted (Kroese 2014, Kühnel 2018), and how to win the evening back.
The 3 AM wake-up: 90-minute cycles, brief awakenings are normal, 'first sleep' and 'second sleep' in history, Wehr's darkness experiment.
Why worries feel bigger at night: the 'mind after midnight', tired amygdala, REM sleep as overnight therapy.
The falling jolt: hypnic jerks, what they are and why they happen.
Why we dream: the main theories and what dream research actually shows.
Sleep paralysis and the 'night visitor': what happens in the brain, why it feels so real.
How sleep saves your memories: replay during deep sleep and learning studies.
The night-time cleaning crew: the glymphatic system and what it clears.
Night owls vs early birds: chronotypes, genes, teenagers and social jet lag.
What your phone really does to your sleep: light, content and what the evidence says.
A better night tonight: practical takeaways, callback to the opening, teaser for the next video.
